questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A patient presents with signs of clinical hypercortisolism including central adiposity, proximal muscle weakness, and abdominal striae. What is the most common overall cause of Cushing's syndrome?
questions.explanation: Most common overall cause of Cushing's: EXOGENOUS steroids. Among endogenous: Cushing's disease (pituitary ACTH) is most common.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: According to the American Diabetes Association (ADA) diagnostic criteria, what is the threshold minimum value for fasting plasma glucose (FPG) to confirm a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
questions.explanation: Diabetes: FPG ≥7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL), 2h OGTT ≥11.1 mmol/L, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or random glucose ≥11.1 with symptoms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A genetic screen reveals a gain-of-function mutation in the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). This pathology causes Liddle syndrome. Which clinical profile is characteristically seen in these patients?
questions.explanation: Liddle syndrome: gain-of-function ENaC mutation → Na retention → hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, LOW aldosterone/renin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A clinician is attempting to differentiate Gitelman syndrome from Bartter syndrome in an outpatient workup. Which of the following features serves as a clear separating marker?

options.A: Gitelman has hypocalciuria, Bartter has hypercalciuria

questions.explanation: Gitelman: NCCT mutation, hypocalciuria, hypomagnesemia, presents in adults. Bartter: NKCC2/ROMK/CIC-Kb, hypercalciuria, presents in infancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 9-year-old child presents with growth retardation and signs of diabetes insipidus. Imaging confirms a benign suprasellar craniopharyngioma. What is the most common clinical presentation of this mass in children?
questions.explanation: Craniopharyngioma: bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression), growth failure (GH deficiency), DI. Calcification on imaging is classic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old female presents with hypermetabolic symptoms and exophthalmos. A diagnosis of Graves' disease is considered. Which autoantibody is directly responsible for driving this pathogenesis?
questions.explanation: Graves' disease: TRAb (TSI — thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin) stimulates TSH receptor → hyperthyroidism. Also anti-TPO may be positive.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A patient experiences an aggressive progression of an ACTH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma alongside severe cutaneous hyperpigmentation. Nelson's syndrome is diagnosed. This condition classically follows which surgical intervention?
questions.explanation: Nelson's syndrome: bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's disease → loss of cortisol feedback → rapid ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor growth + hyperpigmentation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old pregnant female at 12 weeks gestation presents with classic symptoms of hyperthyroidism, including palpitations and heat intolerance. Serum labs confirm a suppressed TSH level and elevated free T4. Which anti-thyroid drug is preferred for management during the first trimester of pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Propylthiouracil (PTU) is preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy due to a lower risk of teratogenic effects (such as aplasia cutis and choanal atresia associated with methimazole). Methimazole is typically switched back in the second and third trimesters to reduce the risk of PTU-induced hepatotoxicity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 48-year-old female presents with recurrent nephrolithiasis, generalized bone pain, and abdominal discomfort. Serum biochemistries demonstrate a corrected calcium of 11.8 mg/dL, a phosphorus of 2.1 mg/dL, and an inappropriately elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) level. What is the definitive management for this patient's condition, and what specific skeletal lesion is classically associated with its long-term progression?

options.A: Aggressive daily oral administration of high-dose Vitamin D3; Osteopetrosis
options.B: Surgical parathyroidectomy; Osteitis fibrosa cystica (Brown tumors)
options.C: Long-term subcutaneous calcitonin injections; Osteitis deformans

questions.explanation: The clinical presentation (hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, elevated PTH) is diagnostic of primary hyperparathyroidism, most commonly caused by a solitary parathyroid adenoma. The definitive treatment for symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism is a surgical parathyroidectomy. Prolonged unmitigated hyperparathyroidism causes extreme bone resorption, leading to osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as 'brown tumors'.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 26-year-old female undergoes screening due to a strong family history of neuroendocrine tumors. Clinical testing reveals a medullary thyroid carcinoma and a unilateral pheochromocytoma. A germline mutation in the RET proto-oncogene is confirmed. This clinical constellation is characteristic of which syndromic classification?

options.A: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN 1 / Wermer syndrome)
options.B: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2A (MEN 2A / Sipple syndrome)

questions.explanation: MEN 2A (Sipple syndrome) is characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism, driven by germline gain-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. MEN 2B also features medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma but is distinguished by mucosal neuromas and a marfanoid habitus, lacking hyperparathyroidism.
